In [[mathematics]], an '''abstract differential equation''' is a [[differential equation]] in which the unknown [[Function (mathematics)|function]] and its derivatives take values in some generic abstract space (a [[Hilbert space]], a [[Banach space]], etc.). Equations of this kind arise e.g. in the study of [[partial differential equation]]s: if to one of the variables is given a privileged position (e.g. time, in [[Heat equation|heat]] or [[Wave equation|wave]] equations) and all the others are put together, an ordinary "differential" equation with respect to the variable which was put in evidence is obtained. Adding [[boundary condition]]s can often be translated in terms of considering solutions in some convenient function spaces.

The classical abstract differential equation which is most frequently encountered is the equation<ref name="abstract">{{cite web |last1=Dezin |first1=A.A. |title=Differential equation, abstract |url=http://www.encyclopediaofmath.org/index.php?title=Differential_equation,_abstract&oldid=14482 |website=Encyclopedia of Mathematics}}</ref> 
:<math>\frac{\mathrm{d}u}{\mathrm{d}t}=Au+f</math>
where the unknown function <math>u=u(t)</math> belongs to some [[function space]] <math>X</math>, <math>0\le t\le T \le \infin</math> and <math>A:X\to X</math> is an [[Operator (mathematics)|operator]] (usually a linear operator) acting on this space. An exhaustive treatment of the homogeneous (<math>f=0</math>) case with a constant operator is given by the theory of [[C0-semigroup|C<sub>0</sub>-semigroups]]. Very often, the study of other abstract differential equations amounts (by e.g. reduction to a set of equations of the first order) to the study of this equation.

The theory of abstract differential equations has been founded by [[Einar Hille]] in several papers and in his book ''Functional Analysis and Semi-Groups.'' Other main contributors were<ref name="zaidman">{{cite book |last1=Zaidman |first1=Samuel |title=Abstract differential equations |date=1979 |publisher=Pitman Advanced Publishing Program}}</ref> [[Kōsaku Yosida]], [[Ralph S. Phillips|Ralph Phillips]], Isao Miyadera, and Selim Grigorievich Krein.<ref name="hille1">{{cite book |last1=Hille |first1=Einar |title=Functional Analysis And Semi Groups |date=1948 |publisher=American mathematical Society|url=https://archive.org/details/functionalanalys017173mbp}}</ref>

== Abstract Cauchy problem ==
===Definition===
Let <math>A</math> and <math>B</math> be two [[linear operator]]s, with domains <math>D(A)</math> and <math>D(B)</math>, acting in a [[Banach space]] <math>X</math>.<ref name="krein">{{cite book |last1=Krein |first1=Selim Grigorievich |title=Linear differential equations in Banach space |date=1972 |publisher=American Mathematical Society}}</ref><ref name="zaidman2">{{cite book |last1=Zaidman |first1=Samuel |title=Topics in abstract differential equations |date=1994 |publisher=Longman Scientific & Technical}}</ref><ref>{{cite book |last1=Zaidman |first1=Samuel |title=Functional analysis and differential equations in abstract spaces |date=1999 |publisher=Chapman & Hall/CRC |isbn=1-58488-011-2 }}</ref> A function <math>u(t):[0,T]\to X</math> is said to have '''strong derivative''' (or to be [[Frechet derivative|'''Frechet differentiable''']] or simply '''differentiable''') at the point <math>t_0</math> if there exists an element <math>y\in X</math> such that
:<math>\lim_{h\to 0}\left\|\frac{u(t_0+h)-u(t_0)}{h}-y\right\|=0</math>
and its derivative is <math>u'(t_0)=y</math>.

A '''solution''' of the equation
:<math>B\frac{\mathrm{d}u}{\mathrm{d}t}=Au</math>
is a function <math>u(t):[0,\infty)\to D(A)\cap D(B)</math> such that:
*<math>(Bu)(t)\in C([0,\infty);X),</math>
*the strong derivative <math>u'(t)</math> exists <math>\forall t \in [0,\infty)</math> and <math>u'(t)\in D(B)</math> for any such <math>t</math>, and
*the previous equality holds <math>\forall t \in [0,\infty)</math>.
The '''Cauchy problem''' consists in finding a solution of the equation, satisfying the initial condition <math>u(0)=u_0 \in D(A)\cap D(B)</math>.

===Well posedness===
According to the definition of [[well-posed problem]] by [[Jacques Hadamard|Hadamard]], the Cauchy problem is said to be '''well posed''' (or '''correct''') on <math>[0,\infty)</math> if:
*for any <math>u_0 \in D(A)\cap D(B)</math> it has a unique solution, and
*this solution depends continuously on the initial data in the sense that if <math>u_n(0)\to 0</math> (<math>u_n(0)\in D(A)\cap D(B)</math>), then <math>u_n(t)\to 0</math> for the corresponding solution at every <math>t \in [0,\infty).</math>
A well posed Cauchy problem is said to be '''uniformly well posed''' if <math>u_n(0)\to 0</math> implies <math>u_n(t)\to 0</math> uniformly in <math>t</math> on each finite interval <math>[0,T]</math>.

===Semigroup of operators associated to a Cauchy problem===
To an abstract Cauchy problem one can associate a '''semigroup''' of operators <math>U(t)</math>, i.e. a family of [[Bounded operator|bounded linear operators]] depending on a parameter <math>t</math> (<math>0<t<\infty</math>) such that
:<math>U(t_1+t_2)=U(t_1)U(t_2)\quad (0<t_1,t_2<\infty).</math>

Consider the operator <math>U(t)</math> which assigns to the element <math>u_n(0)\in D(A)\cap D(B)</math> the value of the solution <math>u(t)</math> of the Cauchy problem (<math>u(0)=u_0</math>) at the moment of time <math>t>0</math>. If the Cauchy problem is well posed, then the operator <math>U(t)</math> is defined on <math>D(A)\cap D(B)</math> and forms a semigroup.

Additionally, if <math>D(A)\cap D(B)</math> is [[dense set|dense]] in <math>X</math>, the operator <math>U(t)</math> can be extended to a bounded linear operator defined on the entire space <math>X</math>. In this case one can associate to any <math>x_0\in X</math> the function <math>U(t)x_0</math>, for any <math>t>0</math>. Such a function is called '''generalized solution''' of the Cauchy problem.

If <math>D(A)\cap D(B)</math> is dense in <math>X</math> and the Cauchy problem is uniformly well posed, then the associated semigroup <math>U(t)</math> is a [[C0-semigroup|C<sub>0</sub>-semigroup]] in <math>X</math>.

Conversely, if <math>A</math> is the [[C0-semigroup#Infinitesimal generator|infinitesimal generator]] of a C<sub>0</sub>-semigroup <math>U(t)</math>, then the Cauchy problem
:<math>\frac{\mathrm{d}u}{\mathrm{d}t}=Au\quad u(0)=u_0 \in D(A)</math>
is uniformly well posed and the solution is given by 
:<math>u(t)=U(t)u_0.</math>

==Nonhomogeneous problem==
The Cauchy problem
:<math>\frac{\mathrm{d}u}{\mathrm{d}t}=Au+f \quad u(0)=u_0\in D(A)</math>
with <math>f:[0,\infty)\to X</math>, is called '''nonhomogeneous''' when <math>f(t)\neq 0</math>. The following theorem gives some sufficient conditions for the existence of the solution:

'''Theorem.''' If <math>A</math> is an infinitesimal generator of a C<sub>0</sub>-semigroup <math>T(t)</math> and <math>f</math> is continuously differentiable, then the function
:<math>u(t)=T(t)u_0+\int_0^t T(t-s)f(s) \, ds,\quad t\geq 0</math>
is the unique solution to the (abstract) nonhomogeneous Cauchy problem.

The integral on the right-hand side as to be intended as a [[Bochner integral]].

==Time-dependent problem==
The problem<ref name="ladas">{{cite book |last1=Ladas |first1=G. E. |last2=Lakshmikantham |first2=V. |title=Differential Equations in Abstract Spaces |date=1972}}</ref> of finding a solution to the initial value problem
:<math>\frac{\mathrm{d}u}{\mathrm{d}t}=A(t)u+f \quad u(0)=u_0\in D(A),</math>
where the unknown is a function <math>u:[0,T]\to X</math>, <math>f:[0,T]\to X</math> is given and, for each <math>t\in [0,T]</math>, <math>A(t)</math> is a given, [[closed operator|closed]], linear operator in <math>X</math> with domain <math>D[A(t)]=D</math>, independent of <math>t</math> and dense in <math>X</math>, is called '''time-dependent''' Cauchy problem.

An operator valued function <math>U(t,\tau)</math> with values in <math>B(X)</math> (the space of all [[bounded operator|bounded linear operators]] from <math>X</math> to <math>X</math>), defined and strongly continuous jointly in <math>t,\tau</math> for <math>0\leq \tau\leq t\leq T</math>, is called a '''fundamental solution''' of the time-dependent problem if:
*the partial derivative <math>\frac{\mathrm{\delta}U(t,\tau)}{\mathrm{\delta}t}</math> exists in the [[Strong operator topology|strong topology]] of <math>X</math>, belongs to <math>B(X)</math> for <math>0\leq \tau\leq t\leq T</math>, and is strongly continuous in <math>t</math> for <math>0\leq \tau\leq t\leq T</math>;
*the range of <math>U(t,\tau)</math> is in <math>D</math>;
*<math>\frac{\mathrm{\delta}U(t,\tau)}{\mathrm{\delta}t}+A(t)U(t,\tau)=0, \quad 0\leq \tau\leq t\leq T,</math> and
*<math>U(\tau,\tau)=I</math>.
<math>U(\tau,\tau)</math> is also called evolution operator, propagator, solution operator or [[Green's function]].

A function <math>u:[0,T]\to X</math> is called a '''mild solution''' of the time-dependent problem if it admits the integral representation
:<math>u(t)=U(t,0)u_0+\int_0^t U(t,s)f(s)\,ds,\quad t\geq 0.</math>

There are various known sufficient conditions for the existence of the evolution operator <math>U(t,\tau)</math>. In practically all cases considered in the literature <math>-A(t)</math> is assumed to be the infinitesimal generator of a C<sub>0</sub>-semigroup on <math>X</math>. Roughly speaking, if <math>-A(t)</math> is the infinitesimal generator of a [[Quasicontraction semigroup|contraction semigroup]] the equation is said to be of ''hyperbolic type''; if <math>-A(t)</math> is the infinitesimal generator of an [[analytic semigroup]] the equation is said to be of ''parabolic type''.

==Non linear problem==
The problem<ref name="ladas" /> of finding a solution to either
:<math>\frac{\mathrm{d}u}{\mathrm{d}t}=f(t,u) \quad u(0)=u_0\in X</math>
where <math>f:[0,T]\times X\to X</math> is given, or
:<math>\frac{\mathrm{d}u}{\mathrm{d}t}=A(t)u \quad u(0)=u_0\in D(A)</math>
where <math>A</math> is a nonlinear operator with domain <math>D(A)\in X</math>, is called '''nonlinear Cauchy problem'''.
